opening: Maths is built like a wall. Each new idea sits on top of the ideas below it. When a child finds maths hard, it is almost never because they are "bad at maths". Nearly always, one brick lower down is loose, and everything above it wobbles.

This guide shows the bricks in order. For each stage of school it lists what your child should be able to do, in plain words. School years are only a rough guide. Some children move faster and some need more time, and both are normal. What matters is that each skill is solid before the next one is built on top.

If your child cannot yet do something on the list for their age, please do not worry. It simply tells us where to start. Ask your tutor and we will show you exactly which skill we are working on and why.

bands.label: Kindergarten to Year 2
bands.intro: These first years are about one big idea: numbers are real amounts that you can put together and pull apart. A child who truly sees that 8 is 5 and 3, and that 10 and 4 make 14, has the ground floor for everything that follows. Please do not rush to big numbers or to written sums. Count real things at home: stairs, coins, grapes. Ask "how many more to make 10?" in the car. Children who know their numbers to 20 inside out find the later years much easier than children who were hurried.

bands.label: Years 3 and 4
bands.intro: These are the times tables years, and they matter more than any others in primary school. A child who leaves Year 4 knowing their tables, able to add and subtract big numbers with confidence, and understanding what a fraction is, will cope with almost anything that follows. A child who is shaky on these will find Years 5 to 8 a struggle, however hard they try. Five minutes of tables practice most days does more than an hour once a week. This is also when NAPLAN first appears, in Year 3. The best preparation is simply making sure the skills below are solid.

bands.label: Years 5 and 6
bands.intro: If I could choose only two years to get right, it would be these. Years 5 and 6 are the fractions, decimals and percentages years. Almost every student I meet who is struggling with algebra in Year 8 is really struggling with something on this list, most often fractions. The good news is that these skills can be learned at any age. If your child is in high school and cannot yet do some of these, that is very common and we can fix it. It is always faster to go back and fill the gap than to push on without it. These years also lead into the Year 5 NAPLAN and high school entry tests.

bands.label: Years 7 and 8
bands.intro: High school maths moves fast, and it quietly assumes that everything from primary school is solid. This is the stage where letters appear in place of numbers. Algebra is not a new subject. It is arithmetic written in a general way, so a student who is unsure with negative numbers or fractions will find algebra confusing, and it is not their fault. When a Year 7 or 8 student comes to us stuck on algebra, we nearly always find the real gap two or three years earlier, fix that first, and the algebra then makes sense quickly. If marks drop in these years, please do not wait. Small gaps here become large ones by Year 9.

bands.label: Years 9 and 10
bands.intro: In Years 9 and 10 schools place students into different levels of maths, and the level your child works at decides which maths courses are open to them in Years 11 and 12. Some skills on this list are learned by every student. Others, such as solving harder equations and drawing curved graphs, are for students aiming at the Advanced or Extension courses. Your tutor will tell you which ones matter for your child. The pace is quick now, and teachers have little time to go back. If something from earlier years is missing, this is the last comfortable chance to fix it before the senior years. A strong Year 10 makes Year 11 far less stressful.

bands.label: Years 11 and 12 · Standard
bands.intro: Mathematics Standard is the practical maths course, and it is the one most students take. It is about money, measurement, data and planning: pay and tax, loans and interest, reading statistics, and using formulas correctly. In Year 12 it splits into Standard 1 and Standard 2. Standard 2 goes further and its HSC exam counts towards an ATAR. The ideas are not abstract, but the questions are wordy and have many steps, so most marks are lost through misreading, weak percentages or careless calculator work. A steady weekly routine matters more here than last-minute study.

bands.label: Years 11 and 12 · Advanced
bands.intro: Mathematics Advanced is the course for students who may need maths at university: science, engineering, commerce, computing, health. Its centre is calculus, the maths of how things change. Calculus itself is not the hard part. What stops students is the algebra underneath it: fractions with letters, powers, factorising, and solving equations quickly and without errors. A student with strong Year 9 and 10 algebra usually finds Advanced very manageable. A student with gaps there will feel lost by the middle of Year 11. If that is happening, the fastest fix is to go back and repair the algebra, not to do more calculus questions.

bands.label: Years 11 and 12 · Extension 1
bands.intro: Extension 1 is taken on top of Mathematics Advanced, by students who enjoy maths and are usually heading for engineering, physics, computing or maths at university. It moves faster and expects students to prove things, not only calculate them. Because it sits on top of Advanced, any weakness in Advanced shows up here twice. The students who do well are rarely the ones who find it easy. They are the ones who write every step clearly and practise the hard question types until they are routine.

bands.label: Year 12 · Extension 2
bands.intro: Extension 2 is the highest level of school mathematics in New South Wales, taken in Year 12 by a small number of students on top of Advanced and Extension 1. It is close to first-year university maths: a new kind of number, formal proof, harder integration, and the physics of moving objects. Students at this level are already strong. What they need is time, a great deal of practice on long questions, and the habit of writing their reasoning so clearly that a marker cannot misread it.

skills.label: Counting and numbers to 20
skills.line: Count out 15 objects correctly, read and write numbers to 20, and tell you which number comes before or after.
skills.why: Every later number skill assumes a number is a fixed amount; a child still unsure here counts everything by ones for years and never builds number facts.

skills.label: Combining and separating within 10
skills.line: Add and take away with objects up to 10, such as working out that 4 apples and 3 apples make 7.
skills.why: Seeing numbers as parts and wholes is the root of all addition and subtraction; without it children can only count, not calculate.

skills.label: Two-digit numbers: tens and ones
skills.line: Tell you that 47 means 4 tens and 7 ones, and count forwards and backwards past 100.
skills.why: Place value starts here; a child who sees 47 as "a 4 and a 7" will be lost in every written method and in decimals later.

skills.topic: Number bonds to 10 and counting on
skills.label: Number bonds to 10 and counting on
skills.line: Tell you straight away which number goes with 6 to make 10, and name all the other pairs that make 10.
skills.why: Bonds to 10 are the engine of mental arithmetic; without instant recall a child cannot bridge through ten and stays on fingers into high school.

skills.label: Addition and subtraction facts to 20
skills.line: Answer sums like 8 + 5 and 13 − 6 in their head without counting on fingers.
skills.why: Every written method and every times table leans on these facts; slow facts make all later work slow, and reading "=" as "the answer goes here" breaks equations in Year 7.

skills.topic: Three-digit numbers: hundreds, tens and ones
skills.label: Three-digit numbers
skills.line: Read and write numbers up to 1000 and tell you what each digit is worth, such as the 4 in 348 meaning 40.
skills.why: Renaming (235 is also 23 tens and 5 ones) is what makes trading in written subtraction make sense; without it those methods are memorised and misapplied.

skills.label: Adding and subtracting two-digit numbers
skills.line: Add and subtract two-digit numbers in their head, such as 38 + 25, and explain how they did it.
skills.why: This is the first time facts and place value must work together; students who cannot do it mentally rely on written methods they do not understand.

skills.label: Patterns and skip counting
skills.line: Count in twos, fives and tens, and tell whether a number is odd or even.
skills.why: Skip counting is how times tables are first built, and spotting the rule in a pattern is the first step towards algebra.

skills.topic: Equal groups: early multiplication and division
skills.label: Equal groups
skills.line: Work out 4 bags of 5 apples by counting in fives, and share 12 biscuits fairly among 3 people.
skills.why: Multiplication must mean "equal groups" before tables are memorised; children who skip this can recite tables but cannot tell when a problem needs multiplying or dividing.

skills.label: Halves, quarters and eighths
skills.line: Find half and a quarter of a group of objects, such as half of 12 grapes, and explain that the parts must be equal.
skills.why: The idea that fraction parts must be equal, and that halving again gives quarters, carries the whole fractions line; Year 5 fraction trouble very often starts here.

skills.label: Measuring length
skills.line: Measure things with a ruler in centimetres, and tell you that 100 centimetres make 1 metre.
skills.why: Units placed end to end with no gaps is the idea behind every later measurement, and the ruler is the child's first number line.

skills.label: Covering areas with equal units
skills.line: Find how many square tiles cover a rectangle by counting the rows instead of every tile.
skills.why: Seeing a rectangle as rows and columns is the picture behind both the area formula and multiplication arrays.

skills.label: Comparing volume, capacity and mass
skills.line: Find out which of two containers holds more water, and which of two objects is heavier, by measuring and not by guessing.
skills.why: Comparing with equal units is the basis for litres, kilograms and cubic centimetres; without it formal units are only words.

skills.label: Time: clocks and calendar
skills.line: Read o'clock, half past, quarter past and quarter to on a clock with hands, and say the days and months in order.
skills.why: Telling the time is a life skill parents notice first, and the clock face later supports fives, fractions and elapsed time.

skills.label: Shapes, objects and position
skills.line: Name common flat and solid shapes, count their sides and corners, and follow directions using left and right.
skills.why: The words for shapes, turns and position are needed for angles, maps and all later geometry.

skills.label: Sorting, simple graphs and chance
skills.line: Read a simple picture graph and tell you which group has the most and how many more.
skills.why: Reading a simple display and comparing groups is where all later graph and data work begins.

skills.label: Place value to 10 000 and beyond
skills.line: Read, write and order numbers into the tens of thousands, including tricky ones with zeros such as 4 072.
skills.why: Numbers with internal zeros and the "ten times as large" idea are where written methods and decimals go wrong; place value gaps here resurface in every later number topic.

skills.label: Mental addition and subtraction to 1000
skills.line: Add and subtract numbers like 56 + 38 or 403 − 198 in their head and check the answer by doing the opposite.
skills.why: Flexible mental strategies are what let a student estimate, check and catch their own errors; without them every later calculation is a blind procedure.

skills.topic: Written addition and subtraction with regrouping
skills.label: Written addition and subtraction with regrouping
skills.line: Set out and solve written sums such as 346 + 278 and 604 − 258 and get the right answer.
skills.why: The written method is reused for decimals, money and measurement for the rest of school; errors in trading across zeros persist into high school if not fixed here.

skills.label: Equality and missing numbers
skills.line: Find the missing number in a sum like 34 + 18 = ☐ + 20, understanding that both sides must be equal.
skills.why: This is where "=" must come to mean "the same as"; students who read it as "write the answer" cannot balance equations in Year 7.

skills.label: Money and change
skills.line: Add up prices and work out the change from $10 or $20 when shopping.
skills.why: Money is the first place children meet decimals and estimation in real life, and it is the context for most percentage and financial maths later.

skills.label: Multiplication facts for 2, 4, 5 and 10
skills.line: Quickly recall the 2, 4, 5 and 10 times tables and use them to divide, such as 20 ÷ 4.
skills.why: These facts, and the doubling link between them, are the base the harder tables are built from; division is learned as the same facts read backwards.

skills.topic: All multiplication and division facts to 10 × 10
skills.label: All multiplication and division facts to 10 × 10
skills.line: Answer any times table question up to 10 × 10 within a few seconds, and the matching division such as 56 ÷ 8.
skills.why: Tables are the single most load-bearing skill in the chain; fractions, long multiplication, division, factors, ratios and algebra all stall when recall is slow.

skills.topic: Multiplying by tens and solving multiplication and division problems
skills.label: Multiplying by tens and solving multiplication and division problems
skills.line: Work out 6 × 40 in their head and decide whether a word problem needs multiplying or dividing.
skills.why: Extending facts to multiples of ten is the core of written multiplication, and choosing between multiplying and dividing is what word problems test all the way to Year 10.

skills.label: Fractions on a number line
skills.line: Show fractions such as 3/4 or 2/3 on a number line and say how much more is needed to make one whole.
skills.why: Seeing a fraction as a number with a place on the line, not just "pieces of pizza", is what makes comparing, adding and decimals possible later.

skills.topic: Equivalent fractions and fractions greater than one
skills.label: Equivalent fractions and fractions greater than one
skills.line: Explain that 1/2 is the same as 2/4 and 4/8, and count in quarters past one whole.
skills.why: Equivalence is the key that unlocks comparing, adding and simplifying fractions; students without it treat 2/4 and 1/2 as different numbers for years.

skills.label: Decimals: tenths and hundredths
skills.line: Put decimals such as 0.4, 0.35 and 0.09 in order and explain why 0.5 is the same as 0.50.
skills.why: The belief that 0.35 is bigger than 0.4 "because 35 is bigger than 4" is one of the most common and lasting errors; it breaks measurement, money, percentages and rounding.

skills.topic: Measuring length, mass and capacity in metric units
skills.label: Measuring length, mass and capacity in metric units
skills.line: Read a ruler, kitchen scales and a measuring jug, and tell you that 1000 grams make a kilogram and 1000 millilitres make a litre.
skills.why: Reading a partly numbered scale is reading a number line; students who cannot do it struggle with graphs, and the 10, 100, 1000 unit links are the basis of all unit conversion.

skills.label: Telling time to the minute
skills.line: Read any time on a clock with hands, match it to a digital clock, and use am and pm correctly.
skills.why: Time is base 60, not base 10; students who are unsure here cannot do elapsed time, timetables or rates such as kilometres per hour.

skills.topic: Area in square centimetres and square metres
skills.label: Area in square centimetres and square metres
skills.line: Find the area of a rectangle by counting squares on a grid and write it in square centimetres.
skills.why: Area must first mean "how many squares cover it"; students who only memorise length times width confuse area with perimeter for years.

skills.topic: Shapes, symmetry and angles as turns
skills.label: Shapes, symmetry and angles as turns
skills.line: Name four-sided shapes such as a rhombus and a trapezium, find right angles, and draw lines of symmetry.
skills.why: Angle as an amount of turn, compared against a right angle, is the idea a protractor measures; the shape names and properties are assumed in all later geometry.

skills.label: Grid maps and compass directions
skills.line: Find a place on a map using a grid reference such as B4 and describe a route using north, south, east and west.
skills.why: Reading across then up on a grid map is the habit that becomes plotting coordinates on the number plane.

skills.label: Column graphs, surveys and chance
skills.line: Read a column graph where each step means 2, 5 or 10, and say which of two results is more likely.
skills.why: Graph scales that are not one-to-one are where NAPLAN data questions are lost, and "likely or unlikely" is the start of probability.

skills.topic: Large numbers, rounding and whole-number addition and subtraction
skills.label: Large numbers, rounding and whole-number addition and subtraction
skills.line: Read numbers in the millions, round them, and add or subtract large numbers while checking the answer makes sense.
skills.why: Rounding to estimate is the habit that catches calculator and decimal-point errors for the rest of school; multi-step word problems start here.

skills.label: Decimals to thousandths
skills.line: Put decimals such as 0.7, 0.305 and 0.35 in order and tell you what each digit is worth.
skills.why: Students who compare decimals by length ("0.305 is bigger than 0.7") cannot convert units, round, or make sense of percentages and scientific notation.

skills.topic: Decimal calculations: adding, subtracting, and multiplying or dividing by 10, 100 and 1000
skills.label: Decimal calculations
skills.line: Add and subtract decimals such as 4.7 + 2.85, and multiply or divide a decimal by 10, 100 or 1000 by moving the digits.
skills.why: Multiplying and dividing by powers of ten is the whole of metric conversion, the core of percentages, and later scientific notation; "just add a zero" fails the moment decimals appear.

skills.label: Factors, multiples and prime numbers
skills.line: List all the factors of a number such as 24 and tell you whether a number is prime.
skills.why: Factors are what simplifying fractions, finding common denominators, and factorising in algebra are made of; a student who cannot see that 6 divides both 18 and 30 cannot simplify 18/30.

skills.label: Written multiplication
skills.line: Multiply numbers such as 347 × 6 and 46 × 23 on paper and estimate first to check the answer.
skills.why: The area model for 46 × 23 is the same picture as expanding brackets in Year 9; students who only know the steps by rote get no help from it later.

skills.label: Division with remainders
skills.line: Divide a number such as 952 by 7 on paper and explain what a remainder means in a real problem.
skills.why: Division is the weakest of the four for most students, and fractions, rates, averages and algebra all need it; interpreting a remainder is the first real test of reading the question.

skills.topic: Order of operations, number sentences and pattern rules
skills.label: Order of operations, number sentences and pattern rules
skills.line: Work out 4 + 3 × 5 correctly, and find the rule in a number pattern such as "multiply the top number by 4".
skills.why: This is algebra before the letters arrive; working backwards is solving equations, a table rule is a formula, and order of operations governs every expression from Year 7 on.

skills.label: Comparing fractions and equivalence
skills.line: Tell you which is bigger, 3/4 or 5/8, and explain why 1/3 is bigger than 1/5.
skills.why: A student who thinks 1/5 is bigger than 1/3 has no fraction number sense, and adding fractions, ratios, probability and algebraic fractions all fail on top of it.

skills.label: Adding and subtracting fractions
skills.line: Add and subtract fractions such as 3/4 + 1/8 by first making the bottom numbers the same.
skills.why: Adding tops and bottoms (1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5) is the classic error; it carries straight into algebraic fractions and probability in high school.

skills.label: Fraction of a quantity
skills.line: Work out 3/4 of $20 in their head.
skills.why: Fraction of a quantity is what percentages, ratios, probability and rates are built on; without it "25% off" is a button on a calculator and nothing more.

skills.topic: Percentages and their link to fractions and decimals
skills.label: Percentages and their link to fractions and decimals
skills.line: Work out the sale price of a $120 jacket that is 25% off without a calculator.
skills.why: Seeing fractions, decimals and percentages as three names for one number is the idea Year 7 and 8 percentage work, and all financial maths, takes for granted.

skills.topic: Negative numbers and the number plane
skills.label: Negative numbers and the number plane
skills.line: Place negative numbers on a number line and plot a point such as (−3, 2) on a grid.
skills.why: The number line through zero is the base for Year 7 integers, and the number plane is where all graphing of lines and curves happens.

skills.topic: Converting metric units, length and perimeter
skills.label: Converting metric units, length and perimeter
skills.line: Change 3.5 kilometres to metres and 2 400 grams to kilograms, and find the perimeter of a shape.
skills.why: Mixed units are the trap in most measurement word problems, and conversion failures follow students into science, rates and area and volume units.

skills.topic: Area of rectangles and triangles, volume of rectangular prisms
skills.label: Area of rectangles and triangles, volume of rectangular prisms
skills.line: Work out the area of a rectangle and a triangle, and the volume of a box, using the correct units.
skills.why: Area as length times width and volume as layers are the two ideas every Year 7 to 10 measurement formula extends; confusing area with perimeter starts here.

skills.label: Measuring angles and classifying shapes
skills.line: Measure an angle with a protractor and work out a missing angle on a straight line, knowing the angles add to 180 degrees.
skills.why: Angles on a line (180°) and at a point (360°) are the two facts all Year 7 to 10 angle reasoning is built from.

skills.label: 24-hour time, timetables and elapsed time
skills.line: Read 24-hour time such as 1545 and work out how long something lasts, such as from 6:50 pm to 8:25 pm.
skills.why: Elapsed time cannot be done with ordinary column subtraction because time is in sixties; it is needed for speed, rates, wages and timetables.

skills.topic: Reading graphs and describing chance with fractions
skills.label: Reading graphs and describing chance with fractions
skills.line: Read line graphs and column graphs, and write a chance as a fraction, such as a 3 in 8 chance of picking a red marble.
skills.why: Probability as a fraction between 0 and 1, and the habit of reading scales critically, are what Year 7 to 10 statistics and probability assume from day one.

skills.label: Negative numbers
skills.line: Calculate with negative numbers without a calculator, such as −5 − 3 and −6 × −4.
skills.why: Sign errors are the most common reason correct algebra gives wrong answers; collecting like terms, expanding brackets and solving equations all run on integer arithmetic.

skills.topic: Fractions: simplifying, comparing, adding and subtracting
skills.label: Fractions
skills.line: Add and subtract any fractions, such as 2/3 + 1/4, and simplify the answer.
skills.why: Unrelated denominators need a general method, and that same method is exactly how algebraic fractions are added in Year 9 and 10.

skills.topic: Multiplying and dividing fractions and decimals, and rounding
skills.label: Multiplying and dividing fractions and decimals, and rounding
skills.line: Multiply and divide fractions and decimals, such as 3/4 ÷ 2/5 and 0.3 × 0.4, and round an answer to 2 decimal places.
skills.why: Students who believe "multiplying makes bigger" cannot judge whether an answer is sensible, and dividing by a fraction is needed for rates, similar figures and rearranging formulas.

skills.label: Percentages
skills.line: Find any percentage of an amount, such as 35% of $240, and work out a price after a discount or after GST is added.
skills.why: Percentage change, and working back to the original amount, is what all Year 9 and 10 financial maths rests on: interest, depreciation, tax and profit.

skills.label: Ratios
skills.line: Share $60 in the ratio 2:3 and simplify a ratio such as 12:18.
skills.why: Ratio thinking underlies scale drawings, similar triangles, trigonometry, gradient and direct proportion; students who treat ratio problems as subtraction are stuck in all of them.

skills.label: Rates and distance–time graphs
skills.line: Work out a speed in kilometres per hour, compare prices to find the best buy, and read a travel graph.
skills.why: A rate is the first gradient students meet; speed on a distance–time graph becomes the slope of a line in Year 9, and rates drive science and financial maths.

skills.label: Powers, prime factors and roots
skills.line: Work out powers and square roots such as 2⁵ and √81, and break a number like 72 into its prime factors.
skills.why: Numerical index laws are the pattern that algebraic index laws copy; roots are needed for Pythagoras, and "2³ = 6" is an error that survives to Year 10 if not caught.

skills.topic: Algebraic expressions: writing, substituting and simplifying
skills.label: Algebraic expressions
skills.line: Simplify an expression such as 5x + 3y − 2x + y and work out the value of 3a + 4 when a is 5.
skills.why: This is the grammar of algebra; equations, formulas, graphs and every Year 9 and 10 topic are written in it, and a student who thinks 3a means "thirty-something" cannot start.

skills.label: Expanding and factorising
skills.line: Remove brackets, such as changing 3(x + 4) into 3x + 12, and put them back by taking out a common factor.
skills.why: Expanding with a negative in front is the most common error in equation solving, and factorising here is the first step of all quadratic work in Year 9 and 10.

skills.label: Solving equations
skills.line: Solve an equation such as 2x − 5 = 11 and check the answer by putting it back in.
skills.why: Solving equations is the tool used in every later topic, from Pythagoras and trigonometry to formulas, graphs and finance; without it, Year 9 and 10 maths is closed.

skills.label: Tables, rules and straight-line graphs
skills.line: Fill in a table of values for a rule such as y = 2x − 1 and draw its straight-line graph.
skills.why: Linking a rule, a table and a graph is the base of all Year 9 and 10 graph work: gradient, equations of lines, parabolas and simultaneous equations.

skills.topic: Angle relationships and properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
skills.label: Angle relationships and properties of triangles and quadrilaterals
skills.line: Find a missing angle in a triangle or on parallel lines and give the reason.
skills.why: Giving a reason for each step is a student's first experience of proof; the angle facts are assumed in similarity, trigonometry and all Year 9 and 10 geometry.

skills.topic: Perimeter and area of triangles and quadrilaterals
skills.label: Perimeter and area of triangles and quadrilaterals
skills.line: Find the area of triangles, parallelograms and trapeziums, and of shapes made by joining them.
skills.why: Choosing the perpendicular height, and handling composite shapes, is needed for surface area and volume; area unit conversion (100 × 100) is a persistent trap.

skills.label: Circles: circumference and area
skills.line: Find the distance around a circle and the area of a circle using π.
skills.why: Circle formulas are reused for cylinders, cones, spheres and sectors; mixing up radius and diameter, or 2πr and πr², costs marks all the way to Year 12.

skills.topic: Volume and capacity of prisms and cylinders
skills.label: Volume and capacity of prisms and cylinders
skills.line: Find the volume of a box, a triangular prism and a cylinder, and change cubic centimetres into litres.
skills.why: The idea "area of the base times height" is behind every volume in Year 9 and 10; the link between cm³, mL and L is heavily used in science.

skills.label: Pythagoras' theorem
skills.line: Find the missing side of a right-angled triangle, such as how high a 5 metre ladder reaches up a wall.
skills.why: Pythagoras is the gateway to trigonometry, the distance formula and surds; it is also the first topic where algebra, roots and geometry must all work together.

skills.topic: Data: mean, median, mode, range and displays
skills.label: Data
skills.line: Find the average (mean), the middle value (median) and the range of a set of numbers, and read them from a graph.
skills.why: Measures of centre and the effect of outliers are the basis for comparing data sets in Year 9 and 10, and are among the most tested ideas in NAPLAN and school exams.

skills.label: Probability of single events
skills.line: Work out the chance of an event as a fraction, such as the chance of rolling a number greater than 4 on a dice.
skills.why: Sample spaces and complements are the building blocks of two-step experiments, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams in Year 9 and 10.

skills.label: Index laws and scientific notation
skills.line: Simplify powers such as a⁵ × a³ and write very large or very small numbers in scientific notation.
skills.why: Index laws are used in every later algebra topic, compound interest, exponential graphs and surds; scientific notation is used daily in senior science.

skills.label: Surds and fractional indices
skills.line: Simplify square roots such as √50 and leave answers in exact form instead of as rounded decimals.
skills.why: Exact values are expected throughout Advanced and Extension maths: the quadratic formula, exact trigonometric ratios and the distance formula all produce surds.
skills.forWhom: For students aiming at Advanced maths in Years 11 and 12

skills.label: Expanding and algebraic fractions
skills.line: Expand brackets and collect terms, and add fractions that contain letters, such as x/3 + x/4.
skills.why: Algebraic fractions are where a weak fractions background finally stops a student; they appear in equations, formulas, gradient and every senior course.

skills.label: Binomial products and factorising quadratics
skills.line: Expand (x + 3)(x + 5) and do the reverse, turning x² + 7x + 12 back into two brackets.
skills.why: Factorising is the main method for solving quadratic equations and sketching parabolas, and it is assumed from the first week of Year 11 Advanced.
skills.forWhom: For students aiming at Advanced maths in Years 11 and 12

skills.label: Linear equations, formulas and inequalities
skills.line: Solve equations with brackets and fractions, such as (2x + 1)/3 = 5, and rearrange a formula to find a different letter.
skills.why: Substituting into and rearranging formulas is how maths is used in science, finance, measurement and trigonometry; reversing the sign of an inequality is a classic lost mark.

skills.label: Quadratic equations
skills.line: Solve an equation with x², such as x² + 5x + 6 = 0, and find both answers.
skills.why: Quadratics are the centre of Year 11 Advanced maths; a student who cannot solve them cannot find where graphs cross, sketch parabolas, or begin calculus problems.
skills.forWhom: For students aiming at Advanced maths in Years 11 and 12

skills.label: Simultaneous equations
skills.line: Find the two unknown numbers when given two facts about them, such as the price of a coffee and of a muffin from two different orders.
skills.why: Simultaneous equations are the first time students handle two unknowns at once; they are needed for intersections of graphs, break-even problems and senior maths of every level.
skills.forWhom: For students aiming at Advanced maths in Years 11 and 12

skills.topic: Straight lines: gradient, midpoint, distance and equations
skills.label: Straight lines
skills.line: Find the slope of a line between two points and write the equation of a straight line in the form y = mx + c.
skills.why: Gradient is the idea calculus is built on, and y = mx + c is the model for every straight-line relationship in science, finance and statistics.

skills.label: Parabolas and exponential graphs
skills.line: Draw the graph of y = x² from a table of values and tell a straight-line graph, a parabola and a growth curve apart.
skills.why: Recognising the shape that goes with an equation is the start of all senior graph work; exponential curves also model compound interest and population growth.

skills.label: Functions and graph transformations
skills.line: Sketch a parabola such as y = x² − 4x − 5, marking where it crosses the axes and its turning point.
skills.why: Function notation, domain and range, and shifting graphs are the language of Year 11 Advanced and Extension maths from the first lesson.
skills.forWhom: For students aiming at Advanced maths in Years 11 and 12

skills.topic: Direct and inverse variation, and rates of change
skills.label: Direct and inverse variation, and rates of change
skills.line: Solve problems where two amounts change together, such as finding the cost of 10 kg when 4 kg costs $12.
skills.why: Proportional reasoning runs through physics, chemistry and economics, and reading how steepness shows rate of change is the intuition behind calculus.
skills.forWhom: For students aiming at Advanced maths in Years 11 and 12

skills.topic: Financial maths: earnings, tax, interest and loans
skills.label: Financial maths
skills.line: Work out pay including overtime, and how much a savings account will be worth after several years of interest.
skills.why: This is the maths adults use most; compound growth is also the practical face of exponential functions in senior courses.

skills.label: Right-angled trigonometry
skills.line: Use sine, cosine and tangent to find a missing side or angle in a right-angled triangle, such as the height of a tower.
skills.why: Trigonometry is a major part of every senior maths course and of physics; errors here come almost entirely from ratio and equation-solving weaknesses, not from the trigonometry itself.

skills.label: Trigonometry beyond right-angled triangles
skills.line: Find sides and angles in any triangle, not only right-angled ones, using the sine rule and the cosine rule.
skills.why: The sine and cosine rules, exact values and angles beyond 90° are assumed knowledge for Year 11 Advanced and Extension trigonometry.
skills.forWhom: For students aiming at Advanced maths in Years 11 and 12

skills.topic: Similar and congruent figures, and geometric proof
skills.label: Similar and congruent figures, and geometric proof
skills.line: Use the scale on a plan, such as 1 cm for every 2 m, to find real lengths and the missing sides of enlarged shapes.
skills.why: Similar triangles are the reason trigonometry works, and setting out a proof with reasons is the style of argument senior maths demands.

skills.label: Surface area and volume
skills.line: Find the surface area and volume of solids such as prisms, cylinders, cones and balls.
skills.why: These problems combine formulas, Pythagoras, rearranging and units in one question, which is exactly what senior exams and optimisation problems in calculus require.

skills.topic: Data: spread, box plots and scatter plots
skills.label: Data
skills.line: Read and draw a box plot, compare two sets of results, and describe the trend in a scatter plot.
skills.why: Comparing distributions and judging relationships between two variables is the core of Standard and Advanced statistics and of reading research in any field.

skills.topic: Probability: two-step experiments, Venn diagrams and two-way tables
skills.label: Probability
skills.line: Work out the chance of two things both happening, such as drawing two red marbles in a row, using a tree diagram.
skills.why: With and without replacement, and "given that", are where intuition about chance fails; they are the base of all senior probability.

skills.label: Using and rearranging formulas
skills.line: Put numbers into a formula correctly, such as a medicine dose or stopping distance formula, and rearrange it to find a different value.
skills.why: Almost every Standard topic is a formula applied to a real situation; students who substitute or rearrange unreliably lose marks in finance, measurement and trigonometry alike.

skills.label: Linear modelling and direct variation
skills.line: Read and draw a straight-line graph of a real situation, such as a taxi fare, and explain what the slope and starting value mean.
skills.why: Interpreting gradient and intercept in context is the base for simultaneous equations, break-even analysis and lines of best fit in Year 12.

skills.label: Earning money and tax
skills.line: Work out take-home pay from a salary or hourly wage, including overtime, tax and deductions.
skills.why: Tax tables are the first multi-step financial calculation in the course and the model for every later one; they are also a guaranteed exam question.

skills.label: Purchasing goods and budgeting
skills.line: Compare the real cost of purchases, including GST and running costs, and set up a weekly budget from a pay packet.
skills.why: Converting costs to a common time period and handling GST backwards are small skills that recur inside loan, investment and rate questions.

skills.topic: Units, accuracy and perimeter, area and volume
skills.label: Units, accuracy and perimeter, area and volume
skills.line: Convert between units such as square metres and square centimetres, and find areas and volumes of real objects such as a water tank.
skills.why: Unit conversion for area and volume is the most common source of lost marks in measurement, and it feeds rates, scale drawings and trigonometry problems in Year 12.

skills.topic: Time zones and location on Earth
skills.label: Time zones and location on Earth
skills.line: Work out the time in another city or country, and the local time a flight will land.
skills.why: Time calculations in base 60 across a date line combine elapsed time, negative numbers and careful reading, which is the style of the whole Standard exam.

skills.topic: Describing data: displays, centre, spread and outliers
skills.label: Describing data
skills.line: Summarise a set of data with its average and spread, draw a box plot, and spot a value that does not fit.
skills.why: Mean, standard deviation and quartiles are the inputs to z-scores, the normal distribution and bivariate data in Year 12.

skills.topic: Networks: shortest paths and spanning trees
skills.label: Networks
skills.line: Find the shortest route between two places on a network map, and the cheapest way to connect every point.
skills.why: Networks are new to almost every student and are taught from the beginning; the vocabulary and systematic working here are required for critical paths and network flow in Standard 2.

skills.label: Compound interest, investments and depreciation
skills.line: Work out how an investment grows with compound interest and how much value a car loses each year.
skills.why: The compound interest formula with different compounding periods underlies loans, annuities and credit cards; choosing the wrong rate per period is the classic error.

skills.label: Loans, credit cards and annuities
skills.line: Work out the true cost of a loan or credit card, and how regular savings grow over time.
skills.why: Reducing-balance loans and annuity tables are the hardest-marked financial questions in the HSC, and the ones students will actually use as adults.

skills.label: Simultaneous equations and non-linear models
skills.line: Find a break-even point from two graphs, and use curved graphs to model growth, such as a population that rises by 8% each year.
skills.why: Recognising which kind of model fits a situation, and reading answers from its graph, is the algebra strand of the HSC Standard paper.

skills.label: Ratios, rates and scale drawings
skills.line: Use the scale on a house plan to find real sizes and costs, and compare rates such as fuel use or electricity use.
skills.why: These questions combine ratio, unit conversion and area in one problem, and are where otherwise capable students drop marks through one missed conversion.

skills.label: Trigonometry in practical problems
skills.line: Use trigonometry to find heights, distances and directions, such as the height of a building from the angle you look up at.
skills.why: Bearings and the non-right-angled rules in Standard 2 are reliably examined and depend entirely on drawing the right diagram and solving the resulting equation.

skills.topic: Bivariate data: scatter plots and lines of best fit
skills.label: Bivariate data
skills.line: Describe the trend in a scatter plot, fit a line to it, and use the line to make a sensible prediction.
skills.why: Interpreting correlation and the limits of prediction is the statistical reasoning the HSC rewards, and it is the everyday skill of reading claims in the news.

skills.label: Relative frequency and probability
skills.line: Use past results to predict how often something will happen, and find the chance of two events both happening.
skills.why: Expected value and multi-step probability are regular HSC questions and connect directly to insurance, gambling and risk decisions.

skills.label: The normal distribution and z-scores
skills.line: Compare results from two different tests fairly, and say what percentage of results fall within a given range.
skills.why: z-scores are how HSC marks themselves are scaled, and the normal distribution is the single most transferable statistics idea in the course.

skills.topic: Critical path analysis and network flow
skills.label: Critical path analysis and network flow
skills.line: Plan a project with many steps, such as building a house, and find the shortest possible time to finish it.
skills.why: These are long, systematic questions worth many marks; students who are careless with forward and backward scanning lose all of them at once.

skills.topic: Algebraic techniques: indices, surds and quadratic equations
skills.label: Algebraic techniques
skills.line: Simplify expressions with powers and square roots, and solve any equation with x² in it by three different methods.
skills.why: This is the gate to the whole course; every calculus question ends in algebra, and students who are slow or error-prone here cannot finish them, however well they understand the calculus.

skills.topic: Functions and relations: notation, domain and range, composites
skills.label: Functions and relations
skills.line: Use function notation such as f(x), and state the possible x and y values of a graph.
skills.why: Every later topic is written in function language; domain, range and composition are needed for the chain rule, inverse functions and probability density functions.

skills.topic: Linear, quadratic, cubic and reciprocal functions, circles and variation
skills.label: Linear, quadratic, cubic and reciprocal functions, circles and variation
skills.line: Sketch straight lines, parabolas, cubic curves, hyperbolas and circles from their equations and find where two graphs cross.
skills.why: Knowing the shape of a function before doing any calculus is what lets a student check their work; curve sketching, optimisation and areas all assume these graphs are automatic.

skills.topic: Absolute value, piecewise functions and graph transformations
skills.label: Absolute value, piecewise functions and graph transformations
skills.line: Shift, stretch and flip a graph by changing its equation, and work with graphs that follow different rules in different parts.
skills.why: Transformations turn a handful of basic graphs into every graph in the course, and are reused for trigonometric graphs, modelling and the normal distribution.

skills.topic: Trigonometry with any angle, and radians
skills.label: Trigonometry with any angle, and radians
skills.line: Find exact values of sine, cosine and tangent for angles of any size, and measure angles in radians as well as degrees.
skills.why: Radians are required for all calculus with trigonometric functions; a student who thinks only in degrees cannot differentiate sin x correctly.

skills.label: Trigonometric identities and equations
skills.line: Solve equations such as sin x = 1/2 and find every answer in a given range, not only the one the calculator shows.
skills.why: Finding all solutions in a domain is needed for stationary points of trigonometric functions and for modelling tides, sound and other periodic behaviour.

skills.label: Exponential and logarithmic functions
skills.line: Use logarithms to solve equations where the unknown is a power, such as finding x when 3 to the power x equals 20.
skills.why: Logarithms are new to most students and are needed at once for growth and decay, finance questions that ask "how long", and the calculus of eˣ and ln x.

skills.topic: Probability, conditional probability and frequency data
skills.label: Probability, conditional probability and frequency data
skills.line: Work out the chance of an event when extra information is known, such as the chance a student plays tennis given that they play soccer.
skills.why: Conditional probability and independence are the base of the random variables topic in Year 12, and of all statistical reasoning at university.

skills.topic: The derivative: first principles and the rules of differentiation
skills.label: The derivative
skills.line: Find the slope of a curve at any point using differentiation, and find the equation of the tangent line there.
skills.why: Differentiation is the central tool of the course; the chain, product and quotient rules must be automatic before exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions are added in Year 12.

skills.topic: Reading derivatives from graphs, rates of change and motion
skills.label: Reading derivatives from graphs, rates of change and motion
skills.line: Explain what the slope of a graph means in a real situation, such as how fast an object is moving at a given moment.
skills.why: Interpreting the derivative as a rate is what makes calculus useful; it leads directly to curve sketching, optimisation and motion problems in Year 12.

skills.label: Sequences, series and financial applications
skills.line: Find any term or total in a number pattern, and use the same method to work out loan repayments and how savings grow.
skills.why: Series turn finance from table look-up into reasoning, and the annuity and loan derivations are among the highest-mark questions in the HSC.

skills.topic: Trigonometric graphs, modelling and logarithmic scales
skills.label: Trigonometric graphs, modelling and logarithmic scales
skills.line: Draw wave graphs such as y = 3 sin 2x and use them to model real cycles such as tides.
skills.why: Modelling periodic behaviour is the main application of trigonometry in the HSC, and combines transformations, equations and graph reading in one question.

skills.topic: Differentiating exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions
skills.label: Differentiating exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions
skills.line: Differentiate functions involving eˣ, logarithms, sine and cosine, combining the rules where needed.
skills.why: These derivatives, combined with the three rules, are used in every curve sketching, optimisation, rates and integration question in Year 12.

skills.topic: Applications of calculus: curve sketching, optimisation, growth and motion
skills.label: Applications of calculus
skills.line: Use calculus to find the highest or lowest value of something, such as the box shape that holds the most for a given amount of material.
skills.why: This is where the course pays off and where the longest HSC questions sit; each one is a chain of algebra, differentiation and interpretation, so any weak link loses most of the marks.

skills.topic: Integration: primitives and the rules of integration
skills.label: Integration
skills.line: Reverse differentiation to find the original function from its rate of change.
skills.why: Integration is half of calculus; fluent reversal of each differentiation rule is required before areas, continuous probability and motion can be attempted.

skills.label: Definite integrals and areas
skills.line: Use integration to find the exact area under a curve or between two curves.
skills.why: Areas under curves are how continuous probability, distance from velocity and accumulated change are calculated; forgetting that areas below the axis are negative is the classic error.

skills.label: Discrete random variables
skills.line: Work out the average result to expect in the long run from a game of chance, and how much results will vary.
skills.why: Expected value and variance are the ideas that continuous distributions and the normal distribution then extend.

skills.topic: Continuous random variables and the normal distribution
skills.label: Continuous random variables and the normal distribution
skills.line: Find the probability that a measurement, such as a height or a battery life, falls within a given range.
skills.why: This topic joins calculus to statistics and is heavily examined; it is also the statistics most university courses begin with.

skills.topic: Graphs built from other graphs, and harder inequalities
skills.label: Graphs built from other graphs, and harder inequalities
skills.line: Sketch a new graph from a known one, such as its reciprocal, and solve inequalities with x in the denominator.
skills.why: Multiplying an inequality by an unknown denominator is the classic Extension 1 error; reasoning from graphs is the habit that prevents it.

skills.label: Inverse functions and parametric form
skills.line: Reverse a function to find its inverse, and explain when a function has no inverse.
skills.why: Inverse functions are the foundation for inverse trigonometric functions and their calculus in Year 12; parametric form returns in projectile motion.

skills.label: Polynomials
skills.line: Divide one polynomial by another and use the remainder to find its factors and sketch its graph.
skills.why: Polynomial factorisation and root relationships are used in curve sketching, complex numbers in Extension 2, and the multiplicity results in Year 12.

skills.topic: Further trigonometry: three dimensions, compound angles and equations
skills.label: Further trigonometry
skills.line: Use the compound and double angle formulas to find exact values and solve harder trigonometric equations.
skills.why: These identities are used constantly in Extension integration, in vector and projectile problems, and throughout Extension 2.

skills.label: Permutations and combinations
skills.line: Count the number of ways to arrange or choose things, such as the number of different committees possible from a group of people.
skills.why: Counting underlies the binomial theorem and the binomial distribution; careful case-splitting is also the best early training in rigorous reasoning.

skills.label: The binomial theorem
skills.line: Expand a bracket raised to a high power, such as (2x + 3)⁴, without multiplying it out one step at a time.
skills.why: The binomial theorem links algebra to counting and is the algebra behind the binomial distribution in Year 12.

skills.label: Proof by mathematical induction
skills.line: Write a step-by-step proof that a number pattern is true for every whole number, not only the ones checked.
skills.why: Induction is a student's first formal proof technique; the setting-out discipline it demands carries into Extension 2 and university mathematics.

skills.topic: Vectors: notation, operations and the dot product
skills.label: Vectors
skills.line: Add and scale vectors, which are quantities with both size and direction, and find the angle between two of them.
skills.why: Vectors are the language of physics and engineering, and are required for projectile motion here and for three-dimensional geometry in Extension 2.

skills.topic: Motion in two dimensions and projectiles
skills.label: Motion in two dimensions and projectiles
skills.line: Predict the path of a thrown object, including how high it goes and how far away it lands.
skills.why: Projectile motion is a long, high-mark HSC question that combines vectors, integration, trigonometry and quadratics in one problem.

skills.label: Inverse trigonometric functions
skills.line: Work backwards from a sine, cosine or tangent value to the angle, and draw the graphs of these reverse functions.
skills.why: Inverse trigonometric functions supply the standard integrals of Extension calculus and cannot be handled without a firm grip on restricted domains.

skills.topic: Further calculus skills: inverse and parametric derivatives, substitution
skills.label: Further calculus skills
skills.line: Differentiate and integrate a wider range of functions, including by substituting one variable for another.
skills.why: Substitution with correctly changed limits is the core technique of Extension integration, and is assumed in differential equations and in Extension 2.

skills.topic: Further applications of calculus: related rates, volumes and differential equations
skills.label: Further applications of calculus
skills.line: Set up and solve equations that describe how something changes over time, such as how quickly a hot drink cools.
skills.why: Differential equations are the purpose of calculus in science and engineering, and this is the first time students build the model and do not simply verify it.

skills.topic: The binomial distribution and the sampling distribution of the mean
skills.label: The binomial distribution and the sampling distribution of the mean
skills.line: Find the chance of a given number of successes in repeated trials, and explain how reliable the average of a sample is.
skills.why: This is the bridge from probability to statistical inference, the reasoning behind every poll, clinical trial and quality check.

skills.topic: The language of proof, contradiction and counterexample
skills.label: The language of proof, contradiction and counterexample
skills.line: Write a complete logical argument that a statement is always true, or find one example that shows it is false.
skills.why: Proof is the working method of university mathematics; precise use of "if", "only if" and "for all" is assumed by every other Extension 2 topic.

skills.label: Proving inequalities, and further induction
skills.line: Prove that one expression is always larger than another, for every possible value.
skills.why: Inequality proofs are the least routine questions on the HSC paper and the ones that separate the top marks; they cannot be learned by memorising methods.

skills.topic: Complex numbers: arithmetic and the complex plane
skills.label: Complex numbers
skills.line: Calculate with a new kind of number that includes the square root of −1, and show these numbers as points on a diagram.
skills.why: Complex numbers unify algebra, trigonometry and geometry, and are essential in electrical engineering, physics and later mathematics.

skills.topic: Complex numbers: equations, powers, roots and regions
skills.label: Complex numbers
skills.line: Solve equations that have no ordinary answers, and find and draw all the roots of a complex number.
skills.why: Roots of unity and regions in the complex plane are staple long-answer questions that draw on polynomials, trigonometry and geometry at once.

skills.label: Further integration
skills.line: Integrate difficult functions by choosing the right method from several, without being told which one to use.
skills.why: Choosing the technique is the skill; these integrals are needed at once in mechanics, and in every university calculus course.

skills.topic: Vectors in three dimensions, lines and geometric proof
skills.label: Vectors in three dimensions, lines and geometric proof
skills.line: Describe lines and curves in three-dimensional space with vectors, and use vectors to prove geometric facts.
skills.why: Three-dimensional vector geometry is the basis of computer graphics, robotics and university linear algebra.

skills.topic: Mechanics: forces, motion in a line and simple harmonic motion
skills.label: Mechanics
skills.line: Use calculus and Newton's laws to describe how an object moves, including the back-and-forth motion of a spring or a pendulum.
skills.why: Mechanics is where the whole of school calculus is applied to physics; it is the direct preparation for first-year engineering and physics.

skills.topic: Resisted motion and projectiles with resistance
skills.label: Resisted motion and projectiles with resistance
skills.line: Model how air resistance changes the motion of a falling or thrown object, and find its final steady speed.
skills.why: These are the longest and most demanding questions in school mathematics, requiring modelling, integration and interpretation in a single sustained argument.
